title: Ezekiel's Little Sanctuary
hookLine: the home is called a small sanctuary
tomorrow: what turns a kitchen table into an altar?

lines: THE COUCH IS AN OFFICE NOW.
WHAT IF IT WERE A SANCTUARY?
cards: Rooms take on jobs without asking. The couch becomes an office, the kitchen table a mail sorter, the bed a place to scroll until one in the morning. What if a home could be a small sanctuary instead?
The phrase comes from the prophet Ezekiel, speaking to people far from Jerusalem, with no Temple to walk to and no way home.

teach.b: Ezekiel hears God say of the exiles: "yet have I been to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they are come." In Hebrew, mikdash me'at, a small sanctuary.
The Talmud reads it as the synagogues and study houses of exile: the Temple shrinks, but it doesn't disappear.
Jewish teachers have widened it again, to the home: Shabbat candles, a mezuzah on the doorpost, books on a shelf. Not a museum.
A place where something is set apart, even if it's only a corner.
Now, back through the week, in one breath. Shavuot night: awake for the gift. Avot on a summer afternoon: summer sayings.
Before Tisha B'Av: three quiet weeks. On the floor: sit low. Isaiah's first words after: comfort follows.
The diary: the year is yours. A calendar makes time holy.
A small sanctuary does the same for space.

how: A Jewish home can be called a mikdash me'at, a small sanctuary; families mark this with a mezuzah on the doorposts, Shabbat candlesticks, Jewish books and a table set for Shabbat.

o: a small sanctuary: holiness in a home or synagogue
the inner room of the Temple, entered once a year
a doorpost scroll with verses from the Torah

games.q: a sanctuary, made small — tap the pairs.

s: mikdash me'at first meant the home
in Ezekiel it's God's promise to the exiles; the Talmud reads it as synagogues and study houses; later teachers widened it to the home.
Ezekiel's little sanctuary is spoken about people far from Jerusalem
in the countries where they are come.

games.q: your apartment is tiny and shared. a friend says a Jewish home needs real space for anything holy. what does Ezekiel's phrase suggest?
o: a small sanctuary can be small: one corner, set apart.
wait for a bigger place; holiness needs room to work.
a sanctuary only means a synagogue building.
games.why: mikdash me'at: in exile the sanctuary shrinks but doesn't disappear. a corner can be set apart.

practice: Look around and find one corner you could make beautiful: a shelf, a windowsill, the space by the door. Rest your eyes on it for a few breaths, and choose one thing to place there, a candle, a photo, a book that matters.
Notice what changes in a corner once it's been chosen.

wordCard.voice: Mikdash me'at: a small sanctuary, Ezekiel's phrase for holiness in exile, now a name for the Jewish home.

orig.note: Hebrew: a small (or little) sanctuary, from Ezekiel 11:16.

carryVoice: Hold this: holiness can shrink without disappearing, even to one corner. The next room over is the kitchen.

sources.q: yet have I been to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they are come

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud Megillah 29a ('a little sanctuary': the synagogues and study houses in Babylonia)
Later Jewish teaching applying mikdash me'at to the home (customary usage)
